title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 49-58
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 49-58 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A colleague hands you an unmanaged package that adds a single validation rule you will need in your org exactly once. Which statement is correct about that package after you install it?
options: The component belongs to your org, is editable and deletable like anything else, and the originator can never push an upgrade to it.
The component stays locked and can only be changed by the package's originator.
The component can be upgraded automatically whenever the originator releases a new version.
The component is hidden source code protected as the originator's intellectual property.
questions.explanation: An unmanaged package is a one-time copy. Once installed, each component belongs to the target org, editable and deletable, with no link back to the source package and no way to push an upgrade. The managed-package traits of locked components, IP protection, and upgrade paths do not apply.

questions.question: A team is restructuring its own large, tangled org into modular units that ship on their own with versioning and an upgrade path, but they want the metadata to stay editable in the org where it is installed. Which package type fits, and what distinguishes it?
options: An unlocked package, which is versioned and upgradeable like a managed package but editable in the target org with a namespace that is optional.
A managed package, which is versioned and upgradeable but locks the components and requires a namespace.
An unmanaged package, which is editable in the target org but gives no versioning or upgrade path.
A first-generation managed package, which keeps a packaging org as the source of truth.
questions.explanation: Unlocked packages are the 2GP type built for a team's own org estate: versioned and upgradeable, but the metadata stays editable in the target org and a namespace is optional. Managed packages lock components and require a namespace for distribution, and unmanaged packages give no versioning or upgrades.

questions.question: The team plans a production install of a new package version in mid-October. According to release cadence, what should they check first before scheduling that install?
options: Whether their org's maintenance window conflicts with the upcoming major release that lands around that time, and test the packaged components in the sandbox preview window first.
Whether change sets were used to deploy the previous version.
Whether the package has a registered namespace on the AppExchange.
Whether first-generation packaging was used for the package version.
questions.explanation: Salesforce ships three major releases a year (Winter, Spring, Summer), and each lands automatically in every org. The October window overlaps the Winter release, so the architect checks the org's production maintenance window for conflict and uses the sandbox preview window to test packaged components against the new platform version before production.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does pre-launch testing alone fail as a governance control for an AI model, when it works for a normal application?
options: Because a model's output distribution shifts as the data feeding it changes or a vendor releases a new version, so a pre-launch review is necessary but not sufficient and ongoing monitoring is part of the governance structure.
Because model outputs are always correct in production regardless of how they were tested, so testing wastes effort that should go to deployment.
Because a model's behavior is deterministic after ship, so a single pre-launch sign-off permanently guarantees safety.
Because the EU AI Act forbids any testing of minimal-risk systems, leaving pre-launch checks pointless.
questions.explanation: A model is not stable after ship: its output distribution shifts as the data or the vendor version changes, so governance requires continuous monitoring as part of the structure, not just a one-time pre-launch check.

questions.question: A company builds an assistant that drafts outbound replies to customer support cases, grounded in knowledge articles and case data. How should it be classified, and what does that decision require?
options: As unacceptable risk, which requires an outright ban on the assistant.
As minimal risk, which requires no controls at all because it only helps agents.
As a mid tier above minimal risk: it touches customer data and generates outbound content, so it needs review, production monitoring, and human approval on every outgoing draft.
As high risk, which obligates the company to deny every draft automatically.
questions.explanation: Because it touches customer data and generates outbound content it is not minimal risk, but because it does not deny credit or hire it is below the EU Act's high-risk apex; the tier still requires review, monitoring, and human oversight on each draft.

questions.question: A customer complains that an embedded AI assistant sent them an incorrect policy statement last month. To reconstruct what happened, which set of records does the lesson say you need aligned on the same event?
options: Only the final text that was sent to the customer, with no surrounding context.
The platform audit trail of system actions, the AI interaction record of the model's reasoning and retrieved context, and the decision record of the human approval.
Just the vendor contract showing which AI feature the company subscribed to.
Only the encryption key status, since protected data proves nothing went wrong.
questions.explanation: A complete evidence set needs all three: the platform's system-action log, the AI interaction record (prompt, context, model version, generation), and the human approval record, aligned on the same event to reconstruct the failure.

questions.question: A field service company needs its technicians to view assigned work orders and record parts used while working in buildings with no cellular signal. What is the first architecture decision, and why?
options: Whether to use the standard mobile app with Briefcase or the Mobile SDK, because the offline model determines whether you need development or can configure it declaratively.
Which encryption algorithm to use, because encryption is the only decision that matters for offline apps.
Whether to disable offline support entirely, because no mobile app should work without a connection.
Which mobile device management vendor to buy, because the vendor choice determines all offline behavior.
questions.explanation: The first decision is the offline model: the standard app with Briefcase covers internal users doing standard field work with no development, while the Mobile SDK is only needed for complex offline workflows or hardware integration.

questions.question: A driver marks a delivery complete offline while a dispatcher updates the same stop online. When the device reconnects and syncs, what determines which change survives?
options: The conflict resolution policy, such as last write wins or conflict detection with a rule or human resolution, which you choose before you ship.
The order the records were primed to the device, which permanently fixes which edit wins.
The device's battery level at the time of the sync, which decides whether the upload completes.
The number of records in the briefcase, which determines whether the sync runs at all.
questions.explanation: The conflict policy decides: last write wins keeps one change and drops the other, while conflict detection flags the conflict and lets a rule or a human resolve it. You choose the policy before shipping.

questions.question: A technician loses their phone, which holds a week of offline work orders. What protects the data on the lost device?
options: Encryption at rest, a device passcode, and mobile device management that can remotely wipe the app's data.
Storing all data only in the cloud so nothing ever lives on the device.
Relying on the phone's default settings, which already protect all app data by default.
Disabling offline support so no sensitive data is ever stored locally.
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest keeps the data unreadable without the key, a device passcode keeps the key from being trivially accessible, and mobile device management lets the company remotely wipe the app's data if the device is lost.

questions.question: Per the Lesson 52 content, when can you rely on the Salesforce event bus to deliver events in the order you published them?
options: Across all events, regardless of how the publish calls are made
Only within a single publish call that passes multiple events as a batch; across separate publish calls events can arrive in a different order
Never, the bus does not preserve order under any circumstance
Always, but only for Change Data Capture events and never for Platform Events
questions.explanation: SF is explicit: the order of events in a single publish call is guaranteed and stored and delivered in the order they were passed in, but across separate publish requests events can be delivered in a different order, because requests can be handled by different application servers at different rates.

questions.question: A customer's order status stream labels each event with a Replay ID. When the fulfillment subscriber reconnects after a short disconnect, what should it do to recover the events it missed?
options: Add one to its last Replay ID and pass that computed value back on resubscribe
Ignore the missed events and start fresh, since the bus drops anything a subscriber was not connected for

Store the exact Replay ID of its last successfully processed event, pass that stored value back on resubscribe, and let the bus redeliver everything published after it within the 72-hour retention window
Use commitNumber for identity and bump it by one for every reconnect
questions.explanation: Replay works by persisting the last successfully processed Replay ID and resubscribing from that stored position; the bus redelivers everything published after it, for events still within the 72-hour window. Replay IDs are opaque and non-contiguous, so you never compute a new one by arithmetic.

questions.question: Your event consumer sees the same platform event twice and must not double-apply it. Which approach reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Check whether the Event UUID was seen before, then apply the work in a separate later step
Trust the bus never to redeliver, since Salesforce guarantees exactly-once delivery
Identify the event by its Replay ID and skip any event whose Replay ID looks familiar
Make the consumer idempotent: insert the Event UUID into a dedupe object with a unique constraint that is atomic with the work, and upsert the target record gated by a sequence check
questions.explanation: The bus delivers at-least-once, so duplicates are expected. The fix is an idempotent consumer: a unique-key dedupe on the Event UUID, enforced atomically with the work so two concurrent deliveries cannot both pass the check, plus an upsert gated by a sequence check. Identify the event by Event UUID, not Replay ID.

questions.question: A hub's fan-out leg must call five external systems, but one of them is slow and risks consuming the whole latency budget. Per the lesson, what is the correct first design response for a read-side aggregation view?
options: Fire all five synchronous callouts from within the Apex transaction and accept that a slow system delays the whole page.
Move the fan-out off the synchronous request path or cache the composed result, so the hub does not pay the full fan-out cost on every visit.
Split the aggregation into animation the client can run while the callouts complete in parallel.
Increase the Apex callout limit per transaction above 100 to buy more headroom for the slow system.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the cumulative time for external callouts in a transaction cannot exceed 120 seconds, and a slow system eats time the others needed. When latency matters, the fix is caching the composed view or moving the fan-out off the request path, not paying the full cost on every visit.

questions.question: An architect needs a single REST call that creates an Account, a Contact tied to its new ID, and a Case, all together. Which tool and which limit does the lesson direct them to?
options: The Composite resource, which runs up to 25 subrequests in one call with subrequests able to reference each other's results by ID.
A plain external web service call, because Composite only works when every subrequest talks to an external system.
Separate REST calls, because Composite requests cannot reference each other's results.
Composite Graph, because a plain Composite request is capped at five subrequests.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines Composite as letting a single API request carry up to 25 subrequests that Salesforce runs and returns as one response, with subrequests able to reference each other's results by ID. Composite Graph raises the ceiling to 500 for deep dependency trees, and plain Composite allows more than five subrequests.

questions.question: The ERP responds, the WMS times out, and a rep views the Account. What does the lesson say the aggregation service should return, and why?
options: An incomplete response that omits the missing block, so the rep sees only the data that arrived and is not bothered by error details.
Nothing until all callouts complete, so the rep never views a partially assembled record.
The composed view plus a status field that flags the response as incomplete and names the missing source, so the page tells the truth about a partial result.
A full retry of the whole fan-out inside the same transaction until every source responds.
questions.explanation: The lesson's partial-failure rule is to return, alongside the data, a status that says complete or incomplete and identifies which source is missing. A page that silently omits the inventory because the WMS was down is lying to a rep; naming the missing source tells the truth.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Federated Data: Salesforce Connect, External Objects, and When Not to Use Them”, what does query pushdown actually do?
options: It copies every matching row into Salesforce storage so later reads are local.
It translates the WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT clauses into the source system's query and returns only the filtered result set.
It downloads the full external dataset into Salesforce and filters it locally in Apex.
It forces the source system into a synchronous write-back transaction for the matched rows.
questions.explanation: Query pushdown moves the query to the data: Salesforce translates the filters, ordering, and limit into the source's query and the source returns only the matching rows, so only the answer travels back to Salesforce.

questions.question: Which requirement makes federation the WRONG choice according to the lesson's “when NOT to use it” section?
options: Read-only display of a governed credit balance on the Account page.
An Agentforce action that must read external credit data as though it were a native Salesforce object.
A low-frequency read-only lookup of a clean, authoritative source with strict data residency rules.
A read-heavy report that queries a live external warehouse view.
questions.explanation: Einstein and Agentforce features currently operate on native Salesforce objects and do not support external objects as a grounding or activation data source, so a requirement that an agent read external data as native is exactly the case where federation fails.

questions.question: Which combination does the lesson say a reviewer should catch in a design that aggregates across three external objects per transaction?
options: The page layout width limit and the external object field count.
The daily API limit and the refresh token lifetime.
The Apex callout budget and the lack of join support across multiple external objects.
The storage limit on the external data source and the license cost.
questions.explanation: Callouts are capped at 100 per Apex transaction, so many external-object queries stack toward that cap, and SOQL across multiple external objects does not support joins, so the aggregation would have to be reshaped at the source.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the core purpose of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), according to the lesson?
options: Retraining the LLM on enterprise documents so it permanently knows the client's data
Retrieving relevant enterprise data at answer time and grounding each response in the retrieved context without changing the model's weights
Replacing the LLM with a keyword search engine over a vector database
Storing a full copy of all enterprise data inside the model's training corpus
questions.explanation: RAG connects an LLM to an external knowledge base and grounds each answer in the specific, current, authoritative enterprise data that actually answers the question. It does not retrain the model; it changes how the model answers. The model's weights never change and the knowledge store is updated independently.

questions.question: Which failure mode does a stale RAG index produce, according to the lesson?
options: The model refuses to answer because it cannot find any documents
The retrieval layer returns the wrong passages, so the model argues confidently from outdated or irrelevant context
The model bases answers on a frozen copy of the index that cannot be corrected or governed
The index grows faster than the re-embedding job can refresh the source of truth
questions.explanation: A vector index is a derived snapshot over authoritative source documents. When a source document changes, the corresponding chunks must be re-embedded and the index updated. A stale index makes the model answer from outdated spec or policy, and because the answer looks sourced, it is worse than a naked LLM, which is why a re-embedding pipeline that maps each embedding back to its source version is required.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why does the retrieved-context approach get classified as hybrid search on the Salesforce platform, and where should access control sit in the stack?
options: Hybrid search merges rule-based validation with user feedback, and access control sits only on the source system
Hybrid search blends meaning-based semantic search with keyword search to refine results, and access control belongs on the retrieval layer before generation
Hybrid search translates prompts into multiple languages, and access control belongs on the generation output
Hybrid search combines vector and relational databases, and access control is enforced after the answer is written
questions.explanation: Salesforce states semantic search is combined with keyword search to further refine results, the hybrid-search lever described in the lesson. The lesson's governance guidance, reinforced by the federated-data lesson's dual-security point, is that access control belongs on the retrieval layer before generation so a questioner only retrieves the enterprise data they are entitled to see.

questions.question: Two users in your org both read the interface in English. User A has a German (Germany) locale and User B has a United States locale. Which statement best describes what will differ between their screens?
options: Only the words on the buttons will differ; every value will be formatted identically.
The date, time, and number formatting will differ, even though the interface language is the same.
Neither language nor formatting will differ because the interface language is the same.
Every record's currency will automatically convert so each user sees a different unit.
questions.explanation: Locale controls formatting (dates, times, numbers, names, addresses) independently of language, which controls the interface text. With the same language selected, users with different locales still see different value formats.

questions.question: An org has Advanced Currency Management enabled with dated exchange rates. Per the lesson, which of the following conversions does NOT use the dated exchange rate?
options: An opportunity that closed last quarter, valued at the rate in force that month.
An opportunity product line item amount.
A currency formula field result on the opportunity.
A currency amount in a report related to opportunities.
questions.explanation: Dated exchange rates are not used when calculating formula fields with a return type of Currency, nor in forecasting, currency fields on other objects, or other report types. They are used for opportunities, opportunity products, schedules, campaign opportunity fields, opportunity splits, and related reports.

questions.question: An architect changes an Account record's default currency from EUR to USD. Based on the lesson, what happens to the existing currency amounts on that record?
options: They are immediately revalued at the current exchange rate.
They are not converted; they display with the new currency code.
They are converted through the corporate currency in two steps.
The change is blocked unless Advanced Currency Management is enabled.
questions.explanation: Changing the default currency of a record does not convert its amounts; they simply display with the new currency code. The two-step record-to-corporate-to-personal conversion applies when a value is actually converted, not when the record's currency label is changed.

questions.question: WCAG is organized around four principles rather than a symptom list. Which of these is one of those four principles?
options: Perceivable
Optimized
Consistent
Responsive
questions.explanation: WCAG's four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. They are the load-bearing structure of the standard: every success criterion is an expression of one of them.

questions.question: An architect wants a custom status badge that shows an overdue flag using red color alone, because the team likes a color-only presentation. Based on the lesson, which design requirement rules this out?
options: Meaning must not be conveyed by color alone.
All text must meet a 7:1 contrast ratio.
Every badge must use a Lightning base component.
The badge must announce via an aria-live region.
questions.explanation: The perceivability principle and contrast criteria require that color is not the only channel for meaning. The fix is to pair the red with text and an icon that has a text alternative, and to check the red against the 4.5:1 ratio for small text.

questions.question: Why does choosing a Lightning base component resolve most contrast and keyboard work in a Salesforce build?
options: Because base components disable custom styling entirely.
Because base components contain accessible SLDS markup, follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, and meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast.
Because base components automatically pass all WCAG AAA criteria.
Because base components replace the need for real form labels.
questions.explanation: Base components include accessible HTML markup from SLDS, follow the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide for keyboard behavior and ARIA management, and conform to SLDS color guidelines that meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast. That is why preferring base components is the highest-leverage accessibility decision.

questions.question: An architect drafts an NFR that reads "the order page should be fast." Based on the lesson, why does this fail as a non-functional requirement?
options: Because it relates to functionality rather than a quality of the solution.
Because it names no quantity, number, and condition, so no test or reviewer can verify it.
Because the platform SLA already covers response time for customer-facing pages.
Because response time is not a quality that a Salesforce solution can control.
questions.explanation: The lesson's test for a good NFR is that it names a quantity, a number, and a condition. "Should be fast" names none of them, so every reader interprets it differently and no test can be built for it. The measurable form is a target such as "returns a confirmation within two seconds for ninety percent of users at expected peak volume."

questions.question: A customer-facing Experience Cloud order flow calls an external inventory API. The architect writes a reliability NFR but cannot decide between setting a recovery time objective (RTO) and a recovery point objective (RPO). Which statement correctly applies both from the lesson?
options: RPO is how long the solution can be down, and RTO is how much data the business accepts losing.
RTO is how long the solution can be down, and RPO is how much data the business accepts losing; both together define how the solution behaves when something goes wrong.
RTO and RPO are the same target measured at different points in the flow.
An integration callout is covered entirely by the Salesforce platform SLA, so the architect need not set either.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines RTO as how long the solution can be down and RPO as how much data the business accepts losing, and notes that these recovery targets determine how a system behaves when things go wrong. They translate directly into design choices, such as whether a data replication or backup strategy is required.

questions.question: An architect wants the build team to implement an order flow and realizes a stock check can fail or time out. Which sequence diagram technique from the lesson forces the architect to decide, on paper, what happens on the failure path?
options: Adding every participant as a lifeline in the "instance name : class name" form.
Including every return message on a dotted line with an open arrowhead.
Adding an alternative combined fragment labeled "alt" whose guards route to a confirmed path and a manual-review path.
Renaming the frame so it begins with "sd" instead of another diagram type.
questions.explanation: An alternative combined fragment, labeled "alt", models if-then-else logic: it sends one set of messages when a guard is true and a different set otherwise. Drawing the happy path and the failure path inside an alt fragment forces the architect to decide what happens when the third-party system is slow or down, which is the decision that is painful to make for the first time during an incident.
